summary: A 1933 NPS rustic-style two-story lookout above Eunice Lake in Mount Rainier National Park, listed on the NRHP in 1991 and still occasionally volunteer-staffed.

facts.design: Two-story NPS rustic-style lookout, lookout room over ground-floor storage

staffing.status: occasionally staffed by volunteers in summer

access.note: Reached by a maintained NPS trail from the Mowich Lake area; serves as a weekend visitor-contact point.

visit.trail_note: Popular, family-friendly hike from Mowich Lake past Eunice Lake; parking fills in peak season.

facts.agency: National Park Service - Mount Rainier National Park

events.note: Built as one of four lookouts raised in Mount Rainier NP 1932-1934, designed under NPS architect Edwin A. Nickel.
Newly completed structure lost its roof to a windstorm and had to be repaired; it is now secured with cables to deadmen.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, March 13, 1991, as part of the Mount Rainier National Historic Landmark District.
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register, April 13, 2022.

evidence.supports: Built 1933, NPS two-story design under Nickel
evidence.quote: The Tolmie Peak fire lookout was built in 1933 according to the typical National Park style two-story structure. The upper level houses a lookout station with storage at the ground level. The design was prepared under the supervision of Edwin A. Nickel of the NPS Branch of Plans and Designs.

evidence.supports: Named for William Fraser Tolmie, first non-Native in park bounds
evidence.quote: Tolmie was named after William Fraser Tolmie, a member of Hudson’s Bay Company who spent several months living at Fort Nisqually in the early 1800s... subsequently becoming the first non-native to set foot inside the present day boundaries of Mount Rainier National Park.
The Tolmie fire lookout was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in March 1991 and is sometimes volunteer staffed in the summer.

evidence.supports: One of four lookouts of seven built 1932-1934; roof lost to windstorm; secured with cables; visitor contact point; NRHP date
evidence.quote: The newly completed structure lost its roof to a windstorm and had to be repaired. It is secured against strong winds by cables attached to deadmen. The wood-frame structure is used as a visitor contact point on weekends.

evidence.supports: Trail description from Mowich Lake past Eunice Lake, parking crowded
evidence.quote: The trailhead to Tolmie is near Mowich Lake and the area is oftentimes very busy, especially during peak summer months. Parking can be a challenge, so you may need to add a half mile or mile round trip to the hike.
Built in 1933, this typical National Park Service-style 2-story frame cab shows some obvious signs of wear and tear.

evidence.supports: Seven lookouts once stood in the park in the 1930s, only four remain
evidence.quote: In the 1930s, seven fire lookouts stood inside the Mount Rainier National Park Boundary. Now only four remain in each corner of the park.

sources.title: Tolmie Peak Lookout, NHLR detail (registration date)

notes_for_editor: The NHLR registration date (April 13, 2022) was supplied in the queue brief but I did not independently re-verify the exact date text on the live NHLR page beyond the description text captured; treating source 1 and 3 as the same underlying page. No source gave a precise current rental/booking status, so I avoided claiming one; described it only as occasionally volunteer-staffed per NHLR and Wikipedia's 'visitor contact point' language. 2026-10-04 fact-check: the 'seven lookouts once stood' detail was previously cited to sources 1/2 (NHLR/Wikipedia), which don't contain it; it's actually from source 4 (TrailChick) and has been re-cited there. The windstorm/deadmen, visitor-contact-point, and Landmark District sentences were cited to source 3 (the NHLR duplicate), which doesn't contain those details; re-cited to source 2 (Wikipedia), which does.
